title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.

my_variable <- "B01002_001" # median age

section: How big is the margin of error?
text:
How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)

Now sort to see which counties are measured least reliably.

county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

# A tibble: 10 × 4

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = params$state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                     myvarE myvarM   popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                     <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
1 04001 Apache County, Arizona     36.2    0.3  65680    NA
2 04003 Cochise County, Arizona    42.9    0.5 125458    NA
3 04005 Coconino County, Arizona   32.4    0.2 144643    NA
4 04007 Gila County, Arizona       51.4    0.5  53610    NA
5 04009 Graham County, Arizona     34.4    0.3  38860    NA
6 04011 Greenlee County, Arizona   36.1    0.8   9452    NA



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 0.6  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 1.2 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence          6       1109652.
2 Low confidence           2         13028.
3 Moderate                 7         83458.


This table clearly shows that ACS estimates for median age are least reliable in counties with small populations. The relative margin of error is highest in small counties and decreases as counties grow in mean population.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
We know the least about the two smallest counties in Arizona, Greenlee and La Paz, which make up the “low confidence” moe_pct category. The ACS samples 2-3% of U.S. households annually – and response rates are lower than that – so in Greenlee, with a population of 9,452, the 5-year estimate is likely based on only a couple hundred households. This leads to a higher sampling error than in larger counties.
Since sparsely populated counties have the highest sampling error, their estimates are noisier than those in denser areas. Maricopa County, which is one of the largest counties in the United States, has an moe_pct of only 0.27%, meaning we’re 95% certain that the true median age in Maricopa is within ~1 month of the estimate (37.5 years). Greenlee County has an moe_pct of 2.22%; with an estimated median age of 36.2 years, we can only narrow down the true median age to a much wider ~10-month window at the 95% confidence level.
This could have big implications for policymaking. If funding or resource allocation is determined based on a specific cutoff point or threshold, and estimates are treated as equally precise across counties, small counties are most likely to be hurt, since we see more fluctuation and uncertainty in their estimates as a result of smaller sample sizes.

title: Week 3: Plotting w/ ggplot()
text:
Notes

ggplot()
A plot = a mapping of columns in our data to visual properties on the page.
ggplot(data) + : creates blank canvas aes(…) + : column mappings -> structural features of plot geom_*() + : type of chart

which geom_*?

_histogram() : how a variable is spread
_point() : how two variables relate
_boxplot(), _col() : how groups compare
_line() : how things change over time
_errorbar() : how uncertain is a value?




Derived Uncertainty

Cannot just add MOEs together, need to use tidycensus

moe_sum() : when adding estimates together
moe_prop() : when taking one estimate as share of another (parent) estimate
moe_ratio() : when creating ratio of of two (unrelated) estimates

ACS 5-years are an average of the estimates from each of 5 years. When computing change over time, should compare non-overlapping intervals.
Also need to take standard error of differences in estimates to account for MOEs across years.

title: Week 3: Plotting w/ ggplot()
text:
Key Concepts

aes() is only looking for columns w/in data, not “aesthetics” like colors/style/etc.
Where it goes depends on whether we’re calling ggplot() alone or piping from existing df into it:

ggplot(df) + aes([plot-wide settings]), or
df %>% ggplot(aes([plot-wide settings])) %>% …

Cannot just add raw ACS MOEs from different geographies together.
When calculating change over time, be conscious of interval overlap in ACS data and account for MOEs in the comparison

library(tidyverse)
library(tidycensus)
library(stringr) # loaded for simplifying tract names
library(gt)
library(sf)





In this assignment, I attempt to recreate this 2018 WHYY article’s analysis on changes to poverty rate across Philadelphia. To do so, I pull two variables from the 2006-2010 and 2013-2017 ACS 5-year releases: B17001_002, total number of people whose income is below poverty level, and B17001_001, total population for whom poverty status is measured. The proportion B17001_002 / B17001_001 = poverty rate.
I based my choice of ACS releases on WHYY’s; they directly reference both: “The latest data are from a five-year survey between 2013 and 2017. Comparisons reflect changes from the 2006-2010 five-year period.” These two periods do not overlap, which allows for valid significance testing on the differences between the two periods.
The ACS data allow me to compute the poverty rate estimate for each tract in Philadelphia in 2010 and 2017, and to estimate the change in tract poverty rates between the two releases. I further aggregate to the neighborhood level to examine whether the trends cited in the WHYY article hold up. The article does not state what neighborhood boundaries were used for analysis; I used the latest set of neighborhood boundaries from OpenDataPhilly. This dataset was last updated in April 2024, which suggests that my replicated analysis is unlikely to line up completely with the original WHYY reporting.


Show code
# Note: I've been using R since ~2019, so wrote a couple functions in this script to simplify pulls + calculations across the two ACS releases of interest.

pull_tracts <- function(yr){
  get_acs(
    geography = "tract",
    variables = params$VARS,
    state = params$STATE,
    county = params$COUNTY,
    year = yr,
    survey = "acs5"
  ) %>%
  #   # drop tract name
  # select(-NAME) %>%
  # pivot wider so one entry per tract
  pivot_wider(names_from = variable, 
              values_from = c(estimate, moe)) %>%
  # rename vars for clarity
  rename(est_denom = estimate_B17001_001,
         moe_denom = moe_B17001_001,
         est_numer = estimate_B17001_002,
         moe_numer = moe_B17001_002) %>%
  
  mutate(pov_rate = est_numer/est_denom,
         pov_rate_moe = moe_prop(est_numer, est_denom, 
                                 moe_numer, moe_denom))
}




The 2010 ACS release produces 7 tracts with 0 population; the 2017 release produces 8, displayed below. Examining the tracts using Google Data Commons, I find that all of the tracts represent nonresidential areas – near the airport, in waterfront areas, or encompassing parks. Each of these tracts are dropped from the analysis because they’ll produce NA values due to the zero denominators.
Tract 9806 (also highlighted below) is the one tract in which residents were surveyed in 2010 but not in 2017; we can see that its population was only 92 in 2010, and it had an extremely high MOE relative to the estimate. This small tract is not dropped since it can feed the aggregate neighborhood totals without causing merge issues or data quality concerns.

title: Verify the Claim:
text:
Coefficient of variation
Here, I calculate the coefficient of variation for each neighborhood. Using Jurjevich et al. (2018) thresholds, I report how many neighborhoods fell into each reliability bucket in each ACS release.


Show code
# Add flags according to reliability of estimate
# cv = (SE/estimate) *100
# se = MOE / 1.645
# cv = ((MOE/1.645)/estimate) *100

cv_flag = function(df){
  df %>%
    mutate(cv = ((pov_rate_moe/1.645)/pov_rate) * 100,
         emoji = case_when(
           cv < 12 ~ "😁",
           cv >= 12 & cv <40 ~ "🤨",
           cv >= 40 ~ "🤥"
           ),
         reliability = factor(
           case_when(
           cv < 12 ~ "Reliable",
           cv >= 12 & cv <40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
           cv >= 40 ~ "Unreliable"
           ),
           # ordered factor for table
           levels = c("Reliable", "Somewhat reliable", "Unreliable"),
           ordered = TRUE
           )
         )
}

acs5_2010_hoods <- cv_flag(acs5_2010_hoods)
acs5_2017_hoods <- cv_flag(acs5_2017_hoods)




Show code
# Build reliability table
reliability_table <- full_join(
  count(acs5_2010_hoods, emoji, reliability, name = "n_2010"),
  count(acs5_2017_hoods, emoji, reliability, name = "n_2017"),
  by = c("emoji", "reliability")
  ) %>%
  arrange(reliability)

reliability_table %>%
  gt() %>%
  cols_label(
    emoji = "",
    reliability = "Reliability",
    n_2010 = "2010 (n)",
    n_2017 = "2017 (n)"
  ) %>%
  cols_align(align = "left",
             columns = c(emoji, reliability, n_2010, n_2017)) %>%

With each tract assigned to its neighborhood, I aggregated B17001_001 and B17001_002 estimates and MOEs up to the neighborhood level and calculated neighborhood poverty rates and MOEs.

# aggregate tracts to neighborhood level
agg_hood <- function(df){
  df %>%
    group_by(neighborhood) %>%
    summarize(
      est_numer = sum(est_numer, na.rm = TRUE),
      moe_numer = moe_sum(moe = moe_numer, estimate = est_numer),
      est_denom = sum(est_denom, na.rm = TRUE),
      moe_denom = moe_sum(moe = moe_denom, estimate = est_denom),
      n_tracts = n()
    ) %>%
    mutate(pov_rate = est_numer / est_denom,
           pov_rate_moe = moe_prop(est_numer, est_denom, moe_numer, moe_denom))
}

Build a half-mile zone around every station and merge the circles into one shape. Remember your units.

station_zone <- stations %>%
  st_buffer(dist = 5280/2) %>%
  st_union()

Pick whole cookies: which tracts don’t touch the zone at all?

outside_zone <- philly_tracts %>%
  st_filter(station_zone, .predicate = st_disjoint)

nrow(outside_zone)

[1] 153


Cut the dough: what share of each tract’s area falls inside the zone?

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(tract_area = as.numeric(st_area(.)))

covered <- philly_tracts %>%
  st_intersection(station_zone) %>%
  mutate(covered_area = as.numeric(st_area(.))) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(GEOID, covered_area)

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  left_join(covered, by = "GEOID") %>%
  mutate(pct_covered = replace_na(covered_area / tract_area, 0) * 100)

Notice: that last step is the left_join() from Part 1b. It’s a join by what (GEOID), used to bring a join-by-where result back into the table. The two kinds of join work together.

Notes

Coordinate Reference Systems

Geographic

live on a sphere
units: degrees
3D models of earth tied to locations on surface via lat, long
angular to center of earth
ex: NAD27, 83; WGS84 - standard for GPS



Projected

cylindrical projections of earth -> 2D flat grid
units: feet or meters
line of tangency: no distortion

further from LOT = much more distorted
can change projection LOT to be more accurate for specific geographies

good for local mapping




Projections
Tradeoffs / different types:
Shape: conformal conic - nice shapes for e.g. Canada
Area: equal-area projections
Distance: equal-distance projections
Direction: Mercator projections

EPSG: cylindrical
EPSG | Name | Units |
2272 | PA southern state plane | feet or meters |
5070 | Albers Equal Area | meters |
4326 | WGS 84 | degrees |


UTM: transverse cylindrical

60 zones, 6 deg each w/ LOT vertical in meters
long states like CA or ID might use UTM since better fit

st_within() : fully within

Below, I attempt to replicate the Where Poverty Has Increased in Philadelphia map from the article, adjusted to reflect only the neighborhoods where findings were significant at the 90% confidence level.
Since the WHYY map appears to differentiate between large and more moderate changes to poverty rate, I set my own threshold to separate significant neighborhoods – first, grouping by the direction of change, then finding the median change in poverty rate among the neighborhoods in each group. Neighborhoods with a greater absolute change than the absolute median change in their group are shaded darker to reflect larger changes; others are shaded lighter to reflect smaller changes. All other neighborhoods (including NA areas like those around the airport) are shaded grey.

# Add flags according to reliability of estimate
# cv = (SE/estimate) *100
# se = MOE / 1.645
# cv = ((MOE/1.645)/estimate) *100

cv_flag = function(df){
  df %>%
    mutate(cv = ((pov_rate_moe/1.645)/pov_rate) * 100,
         emoji = case_when(
           cv < 12 ~ "😁",
           cv >= 12 & cv <40 ~ "🤨",
           cv >= 40 ~ "🤥"
           ),
         reliability = factor(
           case_when(
           cv < 12 ~ "Reliable",
           cv >= 12 & cv <40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
           cv >= 40 ~ "Unreliable"
           ),
           # ordered factor for table
           levels = c("Reliable", "Somewhat reliable", "Unreliable"),
           ordered = TRUE
           )
         )
}

Notes

Machine Learning

Parametric models: assumes functional form, easier to explain/interpret
Non-parametric models: do not assume function form, harder to explain/interpret
This course focused on predictive vs. inferential modeling
Care less about having to explain or interpret model – interested in y_hat
Care less if in an individual predictor is significant. If it boosts predictive power, leave it in

We’ll throw in a lot of proxies and variables to see how they perform.



Models
Rigid <———————————————-> Flexible
|<—–LinReg - L1/L2 - LogReg - Trees - RF - GBM - NNs—–>|


Cross validation
K-fold CV - hold out 1/k folds as test data - calculate RMSE - run k rounds - calculate avg RMSE - evaluate model quality

Part 5: Uncertainty in input data
Our Y is an ACS estimate with its own margin of error. Add the residuals to the table and check whether the biggest misses happen where the estimate is least reliable.

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(fitted_m2 = fitted(m2),
         resid_m2  = residuals(m2)) # added

ggplot(tracts, aes(x = rent_cv, y = abs(resid_m2))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "CV of the median rent estimate (%)",
       y = "Size of the model's miss ($)",
       title = "Are the biggest misses in the noisiest tracts?") +
  theme_minimal()








Stop and look: If a tract’s rent estimate has a CV of 35%, how much of the model’s miss there could be survey noise rather than a model failure? What does that mean for flagging “tracts with rents above expectation”?
At CV = 35%, we would expect the model to miss by ~ $250. But there’s a gap in the residual plot from ~32 - 40% CV, and the entire spread from 20 - 60% CV is sparse; we see the RMSE trend increase here. This means the model is missing information in exactly the area where our estimates are least reliable (high CV).

text:
Part 6: Fit vs. prediction






WarningTwo different CVs



Week 3 CV = coefficient of variation: how noisy is one estimate? Today’s CV = cross-validation: how well does a model predict data it hasn’t seen? Same letters, unrelated ideas.



6A: One train/test split

set.seed(322)
n <- nrow(tracts)
train_idx <- sample(1:n, size = 0.8 * n)

train_data <- tracts[train_idx, ]
test_data  <- tracts[-train_idx, ] # inverse

m2_train <- lm(med_rentE ~ med_incE + pct_renter + pct_ba + n_stations,
               data = train_data)

test_pred <- predict(m2_train, newdata = test_data) # on test

rmse_train <- sqrt(mean(residuals(m2_train)^2))
rmse_test  <- sqrt(mean((test_data$med_rentE - test_pred)^2))

c(train = rmse_train, test = rmse_test)

   train     test 
245.2467 293.1797 


Stop and look: Which RMSE is larger? Why would you expect that? In words: “The model’s typical miss on tracts it hasn’t seen is about $___ per month.”
Test RMSE is slightly larger. We expect this since it’s brand new information to the model - the model wasn’t able to train on any of these observations. The model’s typical miss on tracts it hasn’t seen is about $293.21/month.
Change the seed to any other number and rerun the chunk. Did the test RMSE change? That’s why one split isn’t enough. – Yes

Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia’s open data portal
Many of the city’s datasets on OpenDataPhilly are served through a Carto SQL API. You send a SQL query in a URL, and it sends back data. Ask for format=GeoJSON and st_read() reads the result directly, just like the Indego feed in Week 4.
The pattern:
https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=SELECT ... FROM table_name WHERE ...
Three pieces of SQL are all you need:

SELECT the_geom, column1, column2 chooses which columns come back. Always include the_geom, or you get no geometry.
FROM table_name chooses the dataset.
WHERE ... filters rows. Filter in the query, not in R. Some tables have millions of rows, and pulling everything will be slow or fail.

text:
Part 5: Transforming features
Watch the October 9 recorded lecture before you start this part. Below is a summary to work from.
So far, every predictor has entered the model as a straight line: each additional unit of X changes predicted Y by the same amount, everywhere. Transformations let the model bend. For prediction, the question is simply does the bend lower CV RMSE? For interpretation, each transformation changes what a coefficient means, so you need to know how to read it.






TipTransform predictors, not your outcome



Keep your outcome y untransformed in this assignment. If you model log(y), your CV RMSE comes out in log units and can’t be compared to the other rows in your log. (Predicting a logged outcome well requires back-transforming, which is an A4 topic.)



5A: Logs, for skewed predictors
Many urban variables are skewed: a few tracts have huge values, and most have small ones. Income, density, and counts are typical. A log compresses the long tail, so a model can use the difference between 1 and 10 as well as the difference between 100 and 1,000.


Code
# ggplot(tracts, aes(x = burglary_per_sqmi)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()
# ggplot(tracts, aes(x = log1p(burglary_per_sqmi))) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()








Warninglog(0) doesn’t exist



log(0) is -Inf, and it will break your model. Counts and densities often include zeros. Use log1p(x), which computes log(x + 1), for anything that can be 0.


Reading the coefficient: when a predictor is logged, a 1% increase in X goes with a change of about β/100 in Y, in Y’s units. With log1p, this reading is approximate for small values of X.


5B: Squared terms, for curves
If your scatterplot bends (rising and then flattening, or falling and then rising), a squared term lets the line curve. Write it with I(), which tells R to do the arithmetic rather than read ^ as formula syntax.


Code
# m_sq <- lm(y ~ dist_ch_mi + I(dist_ch_mi^2), data = tracts)
# summary(m_sq)


Reading the coefficient: you can’t read either coefficient alone anymore. The effect of X depends on where you are along X. A positive linear term with a negative squared term means Y rises with X and then levels off or turns down. Plot the fitted curve to see it:


Code
# ggplot(tracts, aes(x = dist_ch_mi, y = y)) +
#   geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
#   geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x + I(x^2), se = FALSE, color = "red") +
#   theme_minimal()

Sometimes a number works better as groups, either because the relationship isn’t smooth or because the categories are meaningful. You can make categories from any variable with case_when() or cut(), and then make sure R treats them as a factor.

The cross-validation helper
This function runs 10-fold cross-validation with the same seed every time, so every model in your log is tested on the same folds. You don’t need to change it. Read it once so you know what it does.


Code
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1: don't drop rows).")
  }
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)
  fit$results$RMSE
}

text:
Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia’s open data portal
Many of the city’s datasets on OpenDataPhilly are served through a Carto SQL API. You send a SQL query in a URL, and it sends back data. Ask for format=GeoJSON and st_read() reads the result directly, just like the Indego feed in Week 4.
The pattern:
https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=SELECT ... FROM table_name WHERE ...
Three pieces of SQL are all you need:

SELECT the_geom, column1, column2 chooses which columns come back. Always include the_geom, or you get no geometry.
FROM table_name chooses the dataset.
WHERE ... filters rows. Filter in the query, not in R. Some tables have millions of rows, and pulling everything will be slow or fail.

This helper builds the URL for you. Spaces and symbols in a URL need encoding, and URLencode() handles that.


Code
carto_get <- function(sql) {
  url <- paste0("https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=", URLencode(sql))
  st_read(url, quiet = TRUE)
}

Part 7: Reflection (about 300 words)
Answer in prose, drawing on your model log (incorporate our words of the day for bonus points. just kidding):

What helped, and what didn’t? Name the feature that lowered CV RMSE the most and the one that disappointed you most. Offer a reason for each.

How much of the remaining error might be uncertainty or statistical noise? Use your last plot.

Your answer:

Logging median household income lowered CV RMSE the most, because income’s relationship with ownership rises sharply at low incomes and then flattens out. A straight line can’t fit that relationship well, but log does. The biggest disappointment was deed transfers per 100 housing units; I expected this to be. a strong predictor but it actually worsened CV RMSE. I thought it would capture home/residential turnover in neighborhoods (e.g., no deed transfers might point to a tract with long-term owners and a high owner-occupancy rate). But once I added a layer for new construction, its coefficient shrank by almost 3/4; construction was a stronger signal.
Holding the other predictors constant, each additional percentage point of single family homes in a tract is associated with about a 0,.57 percentage point increase in owner occupancy. The model predicts 72.3% owner occupancy for Census Tract 263.02, where the actual rate is 70.9%.
There are still large blue pockets in Southwest Philadelphia where the model overpredicts ownership. I wonder if collecting data about subsidized or public housing would help improve predictions here. OpenDataPhilly has a PHA Housing Sites map which I couldn’t pull data from, but they also havr an Affordable Housing Production dataset which might have helped.
My model does the worst in tracts where the outcome is actually measured very well (CV under 25%), and the largest residual appears to be in a tract with a CV ~5%, so sampling noise can’t be the main explanation for these errors. The few tracts with high CV only show moderate residuals. Most of the remaining error seems to come from other variables outside the model rather than uncertainty in the existing data.
